The earlier pages introduced [probability mass functions](probability-mass-functions.qmd) and [probability density functions](probability-density-functions.qmd). We can now ask how to summarize the center of either distribution with one number. We do this by returning to total phone count in the [pinned CMUdict pronunciation table](why-random-variables.qmd#the-pronunciation-entry-outcomes).

```{r}
#| label: load-cmudict-expectation
library(ggplot2)

cmu <- read.csv(
  "data/cmudict/cmudict-pronunciations.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  check.names = FALSE,
  na.strings = ""
)
phone_pmf <- as.data.frame(table(cmu$phone_count))
names(phone_pmf) <- c("phone_count", "entries")
phone_pmf$phone_count <- as.integer(as.character(phone_pmf$phone_count))
phone_pmf$mass <- phone_pmf$entries / nrow(cmu)
phone_pmf$weighted_phone_count <- phone_pmf$phone_count * phone_pmf$mass

expected_phone_count <- sum(phone_pmf$weighted_phone_count)
row_mean_phone_count <- mean(cmu$phone_count)
unweighted_support_mean <- mean(phone_pmf$phone_count)

stopifnot(
  nrow(cmu) == 133854L,
  abs(sum(phone_pmf$mass) - 1) < 1e-12,
  abs(expected_phone_count - row_mean_phone_count) < 1e-12
)

c(empirical_expectation = expected_phone_count,
  row_mean = row_mean_phone_count,
  unweighted_support_mean = unweighted_support_mean)
```

The [**expected value**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html) weights each value by its probability. It is also called the mean of the distribution when the weighted average exists. For a discrete random variable,

$$
\mathbb{E}[X]
\equiv
\sum_{x\in\operatorname{cod}(X)}x\,p_X(x).
$$

Applying this definition to the empirical phone-count PMF gives

$$
\widehat{\mathbb{E}}[X]
=\sum_x x\,\widehat p_X(x).
$$

The displayed computation returns `r sprintf("%.3f", expected_phone_count)` phones. Averaging the distinct support values without their masses instead gives `r sprintf("%.3f", unweighted_support_mean)`, because that calculation treats rare and frequent counts alike.

```{r}
#| label: plot-cmudict-expectation
#| fig-cap: "Each bar is a phone count's contribution to the empirical expectation, x times its empirical mass."
ggplot(phone_pmf, aes(phone_count, weighted_phone_count)) +
  geom_col(fill = "grey65", width = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "Phones in pronunciation",
       y = "Contribution to expected phone count") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

The figure makes the weighting operation visible. A value contributes when it is large, frequent, or both; summing all bar heights recovers the expected phone count.

## Interpreting a value outside the support

The expected value need not be a possible observed value. Phone counts are integers, but `r sprintf("%.3f", expected_phone_count)` is not an integer. It summarizes the empirical distribution rather than describing one dictionary entry.

If $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ were independent draws from this empirical PMF, their sample mean would have expectation $\mathbb{E}[X]$ for every sample size. The [later treatment of Monte Carlo uncertainty](../statistical-inference/monte-carlo-integration.qmd#two-uncertainties) explains the additional conditions under which sample averages stabilize near this value. For current purposes, the expectation is a property of a distribution over pronunciation entries.

## The continuous form

For an absolutely continuous variable $Y$ with density $f_Y$, suppose

$$
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|y|f_Y(y)\,\mathrm dy<\infty.
$$

Its expected value is

$$
\mathbb{E}[Y]
\equiv
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}y f_Y(y)\,\mathrm dy.
$$

The factor $y$ weights the probability density at each value. Absolute integrability guarantees that the expectation is finite. The discrete sum and continuous integral implement the same operation.

## Distribution-family calculations

If $K\sim\operatorname{Geometric}(\pi)$ counts failures before the first success, then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[K]
&=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}k(1-\pi)^k\pi\\
&=\pi(1-\pi)
  \sum_{k=1}^{\infty}k(1-\pi)^{k-1}\\
&=\frac{1-\pi}{\pi}.
\end{aligned}
$$

If $Y\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta)$, then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[Y]
&=\int_0^1
y\frac{y^{\alpha-1}(1-y)^{\beta-1}}{B(\alpha,\beta)}
\,\mathrm dy\\
&=\frac{B(\alpha+1,\beta)}{B(\alpha,\beta)}\\
&=\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}.
\end{aligned}
$$

These equations are derived properties of the corresponding PMF and PDF. They are not definitions of the geometric or beta families.

## Check your understanding

1. Recompute the empirical expectation for `phone_count` from its PMF.
2. Why can the expected phone count fail to be an observed count?
3. Which quantity provides the weights in a discrete expectation?
4. Compare the PMF-weighted expectation with the mean of the raw `phone_count` column. Why must they agree here?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Summing $x p_X(x)$ over the empirical PMF gives $\mathbb{E}[X]=6.380586$ phones. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. An expectation is a probability-weighted average, so it need not be an integer or one of the observed phone counts. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. The discrete expectation uses the PMF value $p_X(x)$ as the weight attached to each possible count $x$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. The PMF-weighted expectation and the raw-column mean both equal 6.380586 because the PMF groups the same 133,854 rows by count without changing their total weight. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>

Expected value averages the original values. The [next page](expectation-of-functions.qmd) asks how to average a transformed property of those values.
